h1: Starting a hard seltzer brand: production and positioning
title: Starting a Hard Seltzer Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: How hard seltzer is made, what the sugar base and flavouring do, the regulatory questions and how to position a seltzer brand without copying the leaders.
teaser: Hard seltzer looks simple: fizzy water with alcohol. The production is more demanding than it seems and the market is crowded.
standfirst: Hard seltzer is a clear, lightly flavoured alcoholic drink. The skill is in the base, the clean finish and a brand that gives drinkers a reason to choose it.
sections:
Most hard seltzers start with a fermented sugar base. A sugar such as dextrose or cane sugar is dissolved in water, fermented with yeast and then filtered to a neutral, clear liquid at a modest strength. Flavour, acid and carbonation are added afterwards. Others use a neutral spirit or a malt base. The route decides how the drink is classified for tax and licensing.

A clean base is the point. Sugar ferments to a thin, neutral liquid with little aroma, so any fault shows. Because the liquid is mostly water, water quality counts: remove chlorine and keep minerals in a sensible range.

Plain sugar and water lack the nutrients that yeast needs. Brewers add yeast nutrient and control temperature and oxygen to avoid stress and off-flavours such as sulphur or solvent notes. A clean fermentation at the yeast's recommended range matters, because there is no malt or hop flavour to hide a fault.

After fermentation the liquid is clarified and filtered. Carbon treatment can strip colour and unwanted flavour. Many producers do this before adding anything back.

Yeast choice matters. A neutral strain at a moderate temperature gives the cleanest result. Warm, fast fermentations make solvent and sulphur notes that are hard to remove. Take gravity and temperature readings daily. Do not rush the finish.

Flavours can be natural extracts, juices or botanical infusions. Citric or other food acids add freshness. Taste at serving temperature and carbonation, because both change how flavour comes across. Seltzer is usually served well chilled and highly carbonated.

Check the flavour supplier's specifications and your market's rules on additives. Test shelf life, because fruit flavours can fade or change colour.

Carbonation is part of the product. Seltzer is usually carbonated to a high level, so tanks, lines and cans must be rated for it. Dissolved oxygen should be kept low at packaging, because oxidation dulls light flavours quickly.

In many countries seltzer falls under a beer, malt beverage, wine or spirit category depending on its base. That sets licences, tax and labels. Rules differ and change, so check with the national regulator or a licensing adviser before you choose a base. See importing brewing equipment if you plan to buy kit. Starting a microbrewery in Africa shows how local conditions change a start-up.

Labels follow from the classification, so decide the base before the design. Warnings, volume and strength statements differ between countries. See what a beer label must show for the common elements.

If you import flavours or packaging, check customs and any additive rules for the receiving country. A flavour that is fine in one market may be restricted in another.

The category is crowded in some markets and new in others. Ask what the drinker is choosing it over: beer, a spirit and mixer, or a soft drink. Distinct flavours, local ingredients, a different strength or a clean, dry finish can all work. Do not make health claims.

Pack choice matters. Cans suit the category and travel well, but need a filling arrangement. A contract canner may be easier than owning a line.

Price against the drinks your customer would otherwise buy. A seltzer priced as a premium craft beer needs a premium reason. A seltzer priced against mainstream lager needs lean production. Decide which you are before you design the pack.

Test with real drinkers before you commit to a pack run. Pour the samples blind next to two competitors, ask which they would buy again and listen to the reasons. A taste that is merely pleasant rarely wins repeat sales.

Think about seasonality. Light, cold drinks sell best in warm weather, so plan stock and cash around the hot months.

Fermentation capacity, filtration, carbonation, a lab and a canning route all cost money. Start with a pilot batch to test taste and stability, then price the cost per litre including packaging and duty. Build in time for approvals of the label and the product.

Our guide to contract brewing explains the contract route, which works for seltzer as well.

Keep a record of every batch: base volume, gravity, fermentation time, filtration, flavour dose, final strength and any losses. Small errors compound. Without records you cannot find them.
faqs: Is hard seltzer made from malt?
Some are, but many use a fermented sugar base. The base affects the flavour, the cost and how the drink is classified.
Do I need a brewery to make it?
You need fermentation, filtration and packaging capacity. A brewery has most of that. A contract partner can supply it.
Strengths vary. Many are low to moderate. Check legal limits in your market.
